Chesapeake Bay Seagrass Coverage, 2012–2019

Total seagrass coverage rose from roughly 19,000 hectares in 2012 to about 43,000 hectares in 2018, then fell to about 27,000 hectares in 2019. Both widgeon grass and eelgrass also fell sharply from 2018 to 2019.

Chesapeake Bay seagrass meadows constitute crucial habitats for many aquatic species. Historically, eelgrass has been predominant, but widgeon grass is proving better suited to recent increases in sea temperature, tolerating heat better and growing faster than eelgrass does. Although the increase in widgeon grass has been associated with a substantial increase in total seagrass coverage in the bay, researchers caution that the latter change does not necessarily make the seagrass ecosystem as a whole more resilient to environmental shocks.

options.text: The scarcity factors imply that all three countries will produce more hydrogen per unit of land by using only solar energy than by using only wind energy, which suggests that the solar coverage scenario is more feasible than the wind coverage scenario; therefore, the student’s claim is fully supported.

France has the lowest scarcity factor for wind among the three countries, suggesting that it will likely need to supplement the use of wind energy with the use of solar energy; therefore, the student’s claim is not supported for France but is for the United Kingdom and China.

The scarcity factors indicate that although France and China would have the capacity to use only solar energy but not only wind energy to meet green hydrogen demands, the United Kingdom would not have the capacity to meet demands using either solar or wind energy; therefore, the student’s claim is only supported for France and China.

The scarcity factors indicate that even though solar energy installations require less land than wind energy installations do, none of the countries will be able to dedicate 10% of available land for solar energy use; therefore, the student’s claim isn’t supported for any of the three countries.
